label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Kelechi,

Yes, I know. You laughed at me on my birthday, told me to put it in writing, and now you're getting a letter through the post like it's 1998. Enjoy it. Read it on the train like you said, and don't pretend you didn't.

I'm not going to preach at you. You've had nine years of people telling you what to do with your life and you have a face for it. So I'll just tell you what I've seen, and you can tell me I'm wrong.

You said at my birthday that every day is the same spreadsheet. I believe you. But I've also watched you explain a cost plan to someone at a dinner table, and I've watched you go quiet when you're bored. You're good at your job. You've always been good at it. After nine years you're still good at it and still bored, and that's not a sign you're bad at it. It's a sign you've got a different itch.

Remember Moremi? Half the hostel was at your door before every exam. You got an A in further maths, and you weren't tutoring because you had to. You liked the moment someone stopped being lost. I was there for a lot of those moments, and you know the face I mean. Everyone gets it, but you were the one who kept going back for it.

Now the school. We're in Peckham, 1,100 kids. Since September, two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them. She's doing her best, and I'm not having a go at her. But supply cover means the kids get a different face every few weeks, and nobody really knows where they are. I'm not saying this to guilt you. I'm saying it because it's real, and because you'd be exactly the person they need.

Then there's Damola. Year 11. He got simultaneous equations after three weeks of me going at it with him. Three weeks. When it finally clicked he shouted "is that all??" and the whole class clapped. He tried to look like he didn't care, and he failed completely. It's the best thing I've seen all year, and I've sat through a lot of staff meetings this year.

And at Christmas, you did fractions with jollof rice portions on plates for my nephew. He still talks about it. He won't remember a worksheet, but he remembers that maths felt like dinner. Kids who think they're "not maths people" are mostly kids who got one explanation that didn't work. You're very good at being the second explanation.

Now the bits I won't sugarcoat, because you'd smell it a mile off.

The money drops in the first year. I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. But you'd be paid while you train, the holidays are proper holidays where you're not checking your inbox, the pension is decent, and the pay scale is published. You can look it up. It goes up on the scale, not on whether your manager likes you.

The hard part is real. I cried in the car park twice in my first term. I'm not hiding that. Marking never ends. Some days behaviour is wahala, and there's a Tuesday period five that will make you want to lie down on the carpet. Some weeks you get home so tired you can't remember what you ate, and that's a kind of tired your spreadsheets never gave you. You'll also have days where you think you've never done anything so right. Both are true. It gets better, but it doesn't get easy. It gets yours.

On your last birthday you said you just want to do something that matters before you're 40. You're 34. That's six years, and you're not too old. A woman in my department started at 41, and nobody in the staffroom treats her like she's late to the party.

And you're wasting yourself checking other people's costings. I'm not having a go at your firm. You're one of the cleverest people I know, and you're using that brain to make sure somebody else's concrete is priced right.

So here's what I'm asking, and it's not a big thing. Come to the open evening on Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I'll come with you. You don't have to sign anything. You don't even have to like it. Eat whatever biscuits they've put out, ask the awkward questions you always ask, and see whether the room makes you feel like you did in Moremi. If it doesn't, you go back to your spreadsheet and I'll never mention it again. I'll only mention it once a term.

Don't reply with a voice note. Reply in writing. I want it framed.

Love you, idiot. Bring the good pen.

[Your name]

---

Posting timing: 19 November is eight days from today, and second-class post from Peckham to Croydon can take two or three days, so it may only just arrive in time. Use first class, or text him that a letter is coming so he doesn't miss it. It's also worth checking the training partnership's site to see whether the open evening needs booking.
